simple.title: Simple integer addition
simple.llvmIR:
define i32 @add(i32 %a, i32 %b) #0 {
entry:
  %a.addr = alloca i32, align 4
  %b.addr = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 %a, ptr %a.addr, align 4
  store i32 %b, ptr %b.addr, align 4
  %0 = load i32, ptr %a.addr, align 4
  %1 = load i32, ptr %b.addr, align 4
  %add = add nsw i32 %0, %1
  ret i32 %add
}
simple.notes: a in %edi (RDI), b in %esi (RSI). Return in %eax (RAX). Single instruction addition.

complex.title: Function with 8+ arguments (stack spilling)
complex.llvmIR:
define i64 @calc(i64 %a, i64 %b, i64 %c, i64 %d,
                 i64 %e, i64 %f, i64 %g, i64 %h) {
entry:
  %mul = mul nsw i64 %a, %b
  %mul1 = mul nsw i64 %c, %d
  %add = add nsw i64 %mul, %mul1
  %mul2 = mul nsw i64 %e, %f
  %add3 = add nsw i64 %add, %mul2
  %mul4 = mul nsw i64 %g, %h
  %add5 = add nsw i64 %add3, %mul4
  ret i64 %add5
}
complex.assembly:
imulq   %rsi, %rdi
imulq   %rcx, %rdx
addq    %rdx, %rdi
imulq   %r9, %r8
movq    8(%rsp), %rax
addq    %r8, %rdi
imulq   %rax, %rcx
movq    16(%rsp), %rax
imulq   %rax, %rcx
addq    %rcx, %rdi
movq    %rdi, %rax
ret
complex.notes: a-g in registers, h pushed on stack (7th and 8th args on stack). Stack offsets 8(%rsp) and 16(%rsp) reference stack-passed arguments.

variadic.title: Variadic function (printf-like)
variadic.llvmIR:
define i32 @sum_ints(i32 %count, ...) {
entry:
  %ap = alloca ptr, align 8
  call void @llvm.va_start(ptr %ap)
  ; ... loop using va_arg ...
  call void @llvm.va_end(ptr %ap)
  ret i32 %total
}
variadic.assembly:
sum_ints:
    pushq   %rbp
    movq    %rsp, %rbp
    subq    $32, %rsp
    movl    %edi, -20(%rbp)
    leaq    -16(%rbp), %rax
    movq    %rax, %rdi
    call    llvm_va_start
    ; ... va_arg loop ...
    call    llvm_va_end
    movl    %eax, %eax
    leave
    ret
variadic.notes: Variadic functions always use all 6 integer registers + 8 XMM registers. va_list is a struct tracking register consumption.

why.question: Why is RDI the first argument register?
why.answer: Historical: System V i386 ABI used stack-based calling. When AMD designed AMD64, they chose registers for the first 6 integer args to avoid stack spills. RDI was chosen first because it is the destination index in x86 string operations (MOVS, CMPS, STOS), and the register assignment follows a logical order from the original 8086 register set. The order RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9 was chosen to match common argument patterns.

why.question: Why does SysV have a 128-byte Red Zone?
why.answer: The Red Zone allows leaf functions to use 128 bytes below RSP without adjusting the stack pointer. This saves a SUB instruction and improves performance for small functions. It is safe because no signal handler or interrupt can preempt a leaf function without first setting up a new stack frame. The 128-byte size was chosen to accommodate typical leaf function local variables.

why.question: Why are some registers caller-saved?
why.answer: Caller-saved registers are volatile: the callee can overwrite them without saving. This gives the callee more scratch registers and avoids unnecessary saves. The caller saves them only if it needs the values after the call. This design reduces save/restore overhead for functions that don't need many registers across calls.

why.question: Why does SysV use 6 integer argument registers instead of 4?
why.answer: AMD64 was designed to improve on i386's stack-based calling. Using 6 registers (vs Windows' 4) reduces stack traffic for typical function calls. Most functions have fewer than 6 arguments, so they avoid stack operations entirely. The extra 2 registers (R8, R9) were added as new registers in AMD64 specifically to support this.

why.question: Why is the stack 16-byte aligned?
why.answer: 16-byte alignment is required for SSE/AVX instructions (MOVDQA, MOVAPS) which fault on misaligned access. It also improves cache line utilization and matches the x86-64 ABI specification. The ABI requires RSP to be 16-byte aligned before a CALL instruction, so on function entry RSP is 8-byte aligned (after the return address is pushed).

flags.description: Sets the compilation target triple. Automatically selects the System V ABI on Linux/macOS.
Explicitly selects the System V AMD64 ABI (default on Linux). Alternatives: ms (Windows ABI).
Generate 64-bit x86 code. Equivalent to --target=x86_64-*. Controls register width, calling convention, and ABI.
Target a specific x86-64 microarchitecture level. Levels: x86-64, x86-64-v2, x86-64-v3, x86-64-v4.
Tune code generation for a specific CPU. Affects instruction scheduling and branch prediction.
Enable SSE4.2 instructions. Available on all x86-64 CPUs (part of the baseline ISA).
Enable AVX2 instructions. Requires --target=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu with appropriate -march.
Enable AVX-512 Foundation instructions. Requires -march=cannonlake or later.
Omit the frame pointer (RBP) in non-leaf functions. Default at -O2+. Frees RBP as a general-purpose register.
Enable the 128-byte red zone. Leaf functions can use 128 bytes below RSP without adjusting the stack pointer.
Disable the red zone. Required for kernel code and functions that use interrupt handlers.
Set the stack alignment. The SysV ABI requires 16-byte alignment before CALL.
